title: Advice to have an open, calm conversation
description: This latent fires on formulaic advice-column recommendations to 'have an open and honest conversation' or 'approach the conversation calmly/respectfully,' typically as a numbered or bolded step in a list of relationship advice (e.g., in response to interpersonal conflicts). It also strongly activates on the bare list markers ('1.', '2.', '3.') that introduce such structured advice steps, suggesting the latent tracks the templated, imperative advice-giving format itself as much as the specific communication-themed content. It does NOT activate as strongly on other sentences within the same advice, such as those offering explanations of the other person's feelings, moral judgments about who is at fault, or general reflections on the situation—those carry related relationship-advice topics but lack the specific 'have a calm/open conversation' imperative phrasing or the numbered-step marker pattern.

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral or bullet token that begins an enumerated list item, typically in advice-giving or step-by-step responses (e.g. '4.', '3. **', '2.'). It activates most strongly on bare digit-plus-period tokens, especially when followed by bold formatting markers introducing a list heading, and to a lesser degree on surrounding list content like suggested actions or considerations. It would not activate on prose sentences without list structure, on numbers used as quantities or dates within running text, or on unordered bullet points lacking a numeric marker.

title: Introducing a numbered advice list
description: This latent fires on the lead-in phrase that introduces an enumerated list of advice, suggestions, or considerations, such as 'Here are some thoughts/points/suggestions to consider:' followed by the start of item '1.'. It activates most strongly on the exact transitional formula plus the beginning of the numbered marker, regardless of the specific topic (relationship advice, financial decisions, workplace conflicts, etc.). It generalizes to related framing phrases like 'Here's my take:' or 'Here's some advice:' that also precede a list, but activates less strongly (random sample) once the list content itself begins rather than the introductory framing. It would not activate on the substantive advice sentences themselves (e.g., explanations, validations, or reasoning about the person's situation) or on list-intro phrases that don't precede an enumerated structure, since the key trigger is the structural cue signaling 'a list of points/suggestions is about to begin'.

title: Calling out passive-aggressive behavior
description: This latent fires on sentences that judge someone's behavior as petty, passive-aggressive, or unnecessarily indirect when a more straightforward alternative was available. It activates on statements that contrast what a person 'could have' or 'should have' done with what they actually chose to do, framing the choice as a moral or social failing. It responds specifically to this critique-of-avoidable-rudeness structure, not merely to descriptions of rude or annoying behavior in general. Sentences that simply narrate an annoying event without evaluative judgment about the person's poor choice of action, or that praise/excuse behavior, would not activate it.

title: Self-help advice list items
description: This latent fires on short, imperative-style bullet-point tips from self-improvement or wellness advice lists, especially those with a bolded keyword/heading followed by a colon and brief explanation (e.g., 'Practice mindfulness**: Focus on the present moment'). It activates most strongly on formulaic prescriptive phrases about mindfulness, positive self-talk, focusing on strengths, deep breathing, and building confidence, and more weakly on other listed personal-growth or cognitive-skill items (e.g., 'Time management', 'Creativity'). It does not activate on conversational, empathetic, or advice-giving prose embedded in full sentences of dialogue (e.g., reassurance, validation, or situational analysis in a Q&A/advice-column format), nor on narrative or discursive text lacking the terse bolded-tip list structure, even if the topic (emotions, relationships, self-care) is similar.

title: Clarifying follow-up questions (advice/chat context)
description: This latent fires on short, generic conversational prompts that solicit more information or elaboration from the interlocutor, such as 'Can you tell me more about what happened?', 'What do you think?', and 'What specifically are you referring to?' It also activates on bare list-item numerals (e.g., '2.', '3.') that likely precede or follow such enumerated clarifying questions in structured advice responses. The common thread is a template-like, open-ended invitation for the user to elaborate on feelings, situations, or intentions, rather than substantive advice, analysis, or declarative statements. It does NOT activate strongly on sentences that provide explanations, give advice, describe reasoning, or make assertions about the situation (e.g., 'It's understandable that...', 'Communicate with your boyfriend...'), even if these appear in the same advice-giving dialogue, since those are content-bearing rather than pure information-seeking prompts.

title: Suggested practical options/resources list items
description: This latent fires on list-formatted suggestions of concrete practical options, services, or resources a person could pursue (e.g., ride-sharing, food banks, community classes, job platforms, housing alternatives, social activities), typically phrased as short bolded headers or bullet fragments naming a category followed by example providers or venues. It activates most strongly on terse, noun-phrase or imperative bullet items ('Explore alternative transportation options, such as public transit or ride-sharing') rather than full advice-giving prose, and is largely topic-agnostic across transportation, housing, food assistance, hobbies, and gig work, unified by the 'here are some concrete options to consider' list structure. It does NOT activate on emotional support statements, moral judgments, relationship advice, or reflective/conversational sentences that lack this enumerated-options-with-named-resources format, even when discussing similar life situations.

title: Hedged partial-agreement openers
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic hedge phrases that open or stand as a reply expressing partial disagreement or qualified negation—especially 'Not entirely.', 'Not necessarily.', 'Not really.'—as well as the recurring 'AITA?/AITAH?' framing question in advice-forum responses. It activates most strongly on these terse, isolated sentence fragments that signal 'the answer is neither a full yes nor a full no' before elaboration follows. It does not activate strongly on the longer explanatory or justificatory sentences that follow such openers (e.g. full reasoning about who is at fault, advice, or validation statements), even though those share the same topic and appear in the same texts; the latent is tied to the compact hedging/qualifying phrase itself rather than to the substantive content of the judgment.

title: Formulaic emotional-support closing statements
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic sign-off lines of encouragement or reassurance—typically imperative phrases like 'Remember,' 'Take care of yourself,' or 'You deserve it'—that closely paraphrase a small set of stock therapeutic-support templates (not alone, deserving of love/respect, prioritize well-being, strong and capable, take care of yourself). It activates most strongly on terse, generic, almost interchangeable reassurance sentences that could close any supportive advice response, regardless of the specific situation being discussed. It activates weakly or not at all on sentences that give concrete, situation-specific advice, ask questions, analyze a person's behavior, or express nuanced judgments (e.g., 'you're partially in the wrong,' 'set boundaries with the homeowner')—even when these touch on similar themes of well-being or self-care, because they lack the stock reassurance phrasing and formulaic cadence.

title: First-person pronoun 'I'
description: This latent activates on the isolated first-person singular pronoun 'I', likely marking the token as the subject-initiating position of a sentence, often at the start of a self-referential statement or personal narrative. It fires specifically on this single word rather than on surrounding context, suggesting a token-level detection of first-person self-reference rather than a thematic or semantic pattern. It would not activate on other pronouns (he, she, they), plural 'we', or on 'I' used in unrelated contexts like abbreviations or Roman numerals, nor on sentences that discuss the concept of selfhood without using the literal pronoun.

title: Empathetic exclamatory framing of a situation
description: This latent fires on short exclamatory openers that characterize an upcoming discussion as difficult, complex, or emotionally fraught—typically of the form 'What a [adjective] situation/dilemma!' used as a rhetorical preamble before advice or analysis. It activates most strongly on these stock templated exclamations (dilemma, tricky, complex and sensitive, heartbreaking, etc.) and more weakly on related empathetic validation statements that acknowledge someone's hard circumstances without the exclamatory 'What a...!' construction. It does not activate on plain declarative advice, factual statements, or supportive statements that lack this framing/summarizing exclamation of the situation's difficulty, even if they discuss similarly emotional or interpersonal content.

title: Acknowledging interpersonal impact on others
description: This latent fires on sentences that frame a situation in terms of its effect on another person (a sister, a child) whose feelings or wellbeing are implicated by the addressee's actions or preferences. It activates on statements that either point out a failure to consider someone else's perspective/impact ('you didn't consider...') or validate a concern rooted in protecting someone else ('it's reasonable that you still don't want your child exposed to...'). These sentences typically appear in advice-giving or interpersonal-conflict contexts, naming a specific third party and the consequence or concern affecting them. It would not activate on purely factual statements, abstract reasoning, or sentences that discuss impact/consequences without referencing a specific interpersonal relationship or third-party welfare.

title: Naming a boundary violation / one-sided imbalance
description: This latent fires on sentences that validate a person's grievance by explicitly framing another party's behavior as disrespecting boundaries, needs, or fairness in an interpersonal or relational conflict. It activates on statements that name the imbalance ('you accommodate, they ignore', 'not respecting boundaries', 'taking advantage') typically in a therapeutic, advice, or mediation-style register that reflects feelings back to a 'you' or 'they'. It does not activate on neutral descriptions of disagreements, factual accounts of events, or conflict language that lacks this validating, boundary/fairness-framing structure -- e.g., simple statements of disagreement or dispute without emotional validation of unfair treatment would not trigger it.

title: Numbered list markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral tokens (and bolded numeral markers like '2. **') that begin items in an enumerated list, most commonly the '2.' or '3.' or '4.' that starts a new bullet point in advice-style responses. It activates most strongly on isolated list-number tokens themselves, and more weakly on surrounding sentences that are part of such enumerated reasoning (e.g., 'Here's why: 1.' or lists of considerations/points). It would not activate on ordinary prose sentences lacking list structure, or on numbers used in other contexts (dates, quantities, prices) that aren't functioning as sequential list markers.
